rv.q: Then suddenly we’re in the offices of the Silicon Valley investment fund run by Paul Montrose (Lloyd Owen) and his protégé May (Millicent Wong), a fifth generation Chinese American.
Challenging, thought-provoking and sometimes gasp-inducingly close to the bone, this relentlessly twisty slice of speculative fiction
This crackling new play is definitely an investment on which Hampstead Theatre should expect a good return.
In cold print it all sounds slightly dotty.
It’s all rather hard to digest in around 100 minutes.
Loeb’s play sparkles when these moral dilemmas are front and centre, the nexus between capitalism and science continually poked and probed, the profit motive necessary but, er,,, cancerous.
Loeb delivers dark humour, twists and turns aplenty, and two gloriously malign central characters to enjoy.
R.O.I. is a worryingly bleak insight into the intersection of medicine and commerce.

In reality, venture capitalists looking for the next futurecorn, unicorn and decacorn investment opportunity, aren’t your typical Dragon’s Den TV investor. Identifying potential multi-$billion returns based on scalability, with short runways and low burn rates, is an art form all its own.
Loeb presents situations that can move quickly from joyful to icy and can sometimes be funny.
All in all, this bleak capitalist drama hits a nerve in spite of its shortcomings.
As R.O.I. questions the cost of progress, Hampstead Theatre’s latest investment proves more than worthwhile in a play rich with ideas, building to an almighty payoff.
Although there is much to think about with this play, I came away feeling Loeb hadn't quite said anything new about the world we are sliding into.

cn.t: Loeb's thought-provoking thriller about venture capital and medical ethics earns praise for tackling big contemporary ideas with dark humor and urgency, though some find its cascade of twists schematic and slightly absurd.
